messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
The forward direction follows from completeness by choosing x_n in F_n, noting that d(x_n,x_m) ≤ diam F_n for m≥n makes (x_n) Cauchy, letting x be its limit in M, and observing that x_m→x with x_m∈F_n for m≥n forces x∈F_n because F_n is closed.
The reverse direction follows by taking a Cauchy sequence (x_n), defining F_n as the closure of the set of x_k with k≥n, noting that these are nonempty closed nested sets with diam F_n→0, taking x in their intersection, and observing that for ε>0, a suitable N puts both x and x_n in F_N for n≥N, so d(x_n,x)<ε.
Does this establish the equivalence?
